Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
The morning after they took the old clock down, people still looked up.

For eighty-three years it had hung over the entrance to the railway station, gaining four minutes every winter and losing them again in the spring. The town had learned to work around it. “Meet me at six, clock time,” someone would say, and nobody asked which clock.

In its place the railway installed a digital display that was accurate to the second. It was useful, especially if you were running. Still, it was mounted lower, and for weeks people glanced up at the four pale bolt holes before remembering where to look.

A woman named Ada bought the old clock at auction for less than she’d expected. She brought it home in the back of a borrowed van and leaned it against the kitchen wall. It was bigger than her kitchen table. For a while she used it to keep the door open.

One Sunday her grandson asked why she’d bought a broken clock.

“It isn’t broken,” she said.

He looked at its hands. “It’s been twenty past three all morning.”

“That’s when your grandfather proposed to me.”

Her grandson considered this. “How do you know it wasn’t sixteen past?”

Ada laughed so hard she had to put down her tea. It was exactly the sort of question her husband would have asked.

The next morning she called a clock repairer. When he came round, he asked if she wanted him to set it to the right time.

“Of course,” Ada said. Then, as he reached for the hands, she asked him to wait until twenty past three.
---

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A compact literary vignette turns a town’s adjustment to a removed clock into a story about memory and love.

## Grounded reading
The voice is gentle and quietly amused, letting affection emerge through ordinary details rather than announcing a lesson. The grandfather’s playful question makes Ada’s memory feel lived-in, and the final pause before resetting the clock invites the reader to see its inaccurate time not as a defect but as part of what it holds.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds public habit and private memory through a single object: an old station clock, its bolt holes, and the time at which a proposal happened. It gives weight to the small rituals people keep after an object is gone, and resolves the tension between accuracy and meaning with Ada’s choice to wait.

## Evidence line
> The town had learned to work around it.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the vignette is coherent and distinctive in how it makes an ordinary object carry both communal habit and intimate history.
